en: The Treatise on the Great Man (Mahāpuruṣa-śāstra),
Volume One, composed by Bodhisattva Deva,
translated by the Northern Liang śramaṇa Daotai.
Chapter One: The Excellence of Giving Homage to the Perfectly Awakened One, the World-Honored One of Great Compassion!
From him arises the True Dharma, the true deliverance within the three realms.
The foremost among the assembly, a treasury of immeasurable merit—
of the bodhisattva’s fundamental practice, I shall now speak a small portion.
Out of compassion for them, I now open and expound the gateway of sublime giving.
All you worthy sirs, you should listen with joy.
When the Bodhisattva practices giving, the great earth trembles everywhere;
the vast oceans well up with myriad jewels, and clouds of wisdom rain down exquisite flowers.
If even those without minds are thus, how much more so those with consciousness?
The Bodhisattva’s giving is vast and expansive, like the realm of empty space;
even if seers possessing the five supernatural powers were to fill the lands of the ten directions, [they could not equal it].
To even hear [this teaching] is difficult; how much more so to explain it in detail?
There is no place where one does not seek alms;
pure water drenches the great earth, reaching everywhere without exception.
There is no object whatsoever that the Bodhisattva has not given away;
there is no sentient being whatsoever who has not received his gifts.
The Proponent says to the Great Earth: "All should pay homage to you."
For what reason do they pay homage to the great earth, the place where the Bodhisattva practiced giving?
In a single day, the Bodhisattva gave away various kinds of manifold things;
even after a hundred eons, a Pratyekabuddha could not know their limit.
Therefore, one cannot know that great compassion is the essence of giving, which can bring about the fruit of omniscience; thus, the cause of giving is the greatest.
This is what the wise have taught: through giving, one can reach the further shore.
If one reaches the other shore, all the perfections (pāramitās) are fully complete.
The meaning of "pāramitā" is called a collective sound,
just as when many people are together, they are called a "great assembly."
The seed of enlightenment, which can bring forth the fruit of great wisdom and is endowed with all requisites for every undertaking, is not accomplished without giving.
Giving is the womb for rebirth in the heavenly realms and the matrix for transcending the world.
Giving without signs is sublime; equanimity is supreme.
Giving both body and possessions without any stinginess, giving in all places without regard for location—this is the highest form of generosity.
Giving at all times, there is no time when one does not give;
among these four kinds of giving, the mind remains ever unmoving.
One who practices giving in this way is said to perform inconceivable giving.
If one gives to a single sentient being, all shall receive happiness;
if one does not give in this manner, it is called deception.
Although it is said that one person is given to, this is in fact giving to all.
Therefore they are called "all," because their great compassionate heart is universal;
the reason great compassion is universal is that it seeks the knowledge of all modes.
To give to Buddhas and Arhats is what the world calls a "noble field of merit."
Giving with equanimity and without sorrow is the most supreme gift.

Giving away immeasurable wealth and treasures does not equal the merit of momentarily ceasing [afflictions] and giving to a single person with a compassionate heart; such merit is like the great earth.
To give everything for one’s own sake yields a reward like a mustard seed;
to rescue a single person from distress surpasses all other forms of giving.
Though the many stars possess light, they do not equal the brilliance of the single moon.
The defiled minds of sentient beings are heavy; whatever they give is always for themselves.
The Bodhisattva gives with a compassionate heart, like ashes removing all impurities;
giving out of rescue and mercy, it is universally for the sake of all classes of living beings.
Such compassionate giving brings merit that is inexhaustible;
through such subtle and wondrous giving, all sentient beings are brought peace and happiness.
Seeking the wisdom of the Buddha, their minds never know satiety.
Thus, the gift of a compassionate heart can remove the obstacles of ignorance and guide those who are deluded and dark, enabling them to obtain the eye of wisdom;
it can extinguish all fetters and subdue old age, sickness, and death.
Giving conjoined with compassion is the nectar for all sentient beings.
When giving arises from great compassion, one’s aspiration is to achieve enlightenment.
One who perceives things in this way is able to accomplish every form of giving.
All such acts of giving ultimately result in the single flavor of wisdom.
Taking great compassion as its essence, it can give rise to various kinds of giving;
by saving sentient beings in manifold ways, one reaches the state of wisdom.
It can eliminate all fetters of craving and the defilement of ignorance;
it enables all sentient beings to attain complete peace and happiness.
Who would not feel love and joy for such a gift of compassion?
If one cannot give rise to love and joy toward the benefits bestowed by the merit arising from the mind of great compassion, but instead turns away from such salvation,
that person is bound by craving; for them, awakening is extremely difficult to attain.
All who seek to become Buddhas delight in giving sweet flavors.
The wise person rejoices in bestowing gifts, for they find joy in the flavor of Bodhi;
seeing deeply the faults of the three realms of existence, they find the flavor of Nirvana to be most blissful.
Swiftly desiring to distance themselves, they do not abide for even a single thought-moment.
Furthermore, seeing that the bliss of giving surpasses even nirvāṇa, they delight in the mastery of giving; their minds then forget bodhi.
When the mind has forgotten awakening, one says that awakening is difficult to attain.
Yet, by observing one's own joyful mind of giving—arising from compassion for sentient beings—one is unaware of the flavor of the joy of giving; for giving possesses three flavors of joy:
First is the flavor of giving that seeks a reward;
second is the flavor of giving that seeks liberation;
third is the flavor of giving that seeks the mind of great compassion.
These three kinds of flavors are called the flavors of increasing joy in giving. Chapter Three:

The Nature of the Donor. When the recipient obtains immeasurable treasures, their heart is greatly rejoiced; however, when the donor performs even a small act of giving, their heart is greatly rejoiced to a degree hundreds of thousands of millions of times greater than that of the recipient.
One who can practice giving in this way performs the foremost deed.
Accomplishing the salvation of others, they drink the nectar of great compassion;
practicing this bodhisattva conduct, they forever eliminate the disease of stinginess and old age.

The bodhisattva’s compassionate mind takes giving as its essence, whereas worldly sentient beings take the fetters and afflictions as their essence; since all are of one and the same flavor of pure suffering, the bodhisattva practices the giving of compassion in order that they may attain happiness.

The sun has illumination as its function; the moon has coolness as its nature; and the Bodhisattva has compassion as his essence. Through wisdom and the giving of material wealth, he brings peace and happiness to all beings. This is like the ten stages of development from the *kalala* stage through to old age: although one reaches old age, one does not abandon the characteristics of infancy.

Just as a bodhisattva’s mind of giving, though parched with thirst, seeks to rescue sentient beings and does not abandon ordinary people—even when free from desire and reaching the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—yet does not depart from the characteristics of ordinary people;
so too it is with the bodhisattva’s non-abandonment of the mind of giving to rescue sentient beings.

To eliminate the thirst for giving, one should drink the water of great giving (*mahādāna*). Although the thirst for giving may be momentarily stilled, other thirsts do not cease, because of one's love for and delight in giving.
All sentient beings subsist by means of food; likewise, great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) subsists by means of giving.

The Dharma-body of a bodhisattva does not depend on food and drink for its sustenance; rather, great compassion serves as their nourishment, and thus the bodhisattva’s body remains. Compassion is like fire, and the desire to give is like hunger; when given excellent food, the bodhisattva delights in giving without ever becoming weary or satiated.
Compassion is like the great ocean and giving is like the Vowoljao (Wojiao) mountain; the mind of rescue and succor is the water, just as the Vowoljao swallows all flowing streams.
Desiring to head toward Bodhi, one takes sentient beings as companions and compassion as the essence, practicing giving without satiety, just as the ocean swallows all rivers without ceasing.
When all sentient beings come, each seeking different things,
the Bodhisattva bestows them all, his mind never weary.
All those suffering from afflictions, he completely eliminates for them.
Even if there are those whose [afflictions] have not yet been removed, the mind never knows satiety.

Chapter Four: The Increase of the Giver and the Beggar. Those possessed of great compassion are able to dwell within birth and death, bestowing various gifts to extinguish the suffering of sentient beings.
If one can do thus, one dwells well within birth and death.
A virtuous man of merit, with hands that bestow grace through a heart of compassion,
pulls those who cannot emerge on their own from the mire of poverty.

Taking compassion as its essence, it is able to practice great giving to extinguish the suffering of sentient beings. Just as a great rain cloud arises during the height of the summer heat, it raises the great compassionate cloud to rain down the hail of giving; it shatters poverty like crumbling mountain rocks. It rescues those in poverty with boundless and impartial giving, causing them to forever leave behind the misery of destitution. With the rain of great giving, it universally benefits all, so that the poverty of sentient beings shall have no place to abide forever.
When a bodhisattva practices giving to save sentient beings, Māra and his retinue all give rise to jealousy, sorrow, and affliction.

When the bodhisattva practices the immeasurable giving of material wealth and the giving of the Dharma, those who are stingy, greedy, and jealous all cry out in alarm; there is none among them who does not feel fear and dread.
With a body made majestic by a mind of loving-kindness, And a thousand eyes formed by a mind of compassion,
Taking up the vajra of generosity, The Bodhisattva is like Śakra,
Capable of utterly destroying The asuras of poverty.
The Bodhisattva’s bow is compassion; With various acts of giving as its arrows, it shatters the enemy of poverty, So that he has no place to dwell forever.
Compassion is its firm root, And kind speech is its stem.
Patience is its branches, and generosity is its fruit.
Those who seek are like birds and deer; the beggar is like a great wind that blows down the fruit of generosity, so that the poor may attain fulfillment.
When the Bodhisattva emerges in the night, his compassionate mind is like the full moon;
taking pure giving as its light, he seeks it like the kumuda flower,
and by means of the radiance of pure giving, he causes it to bloom.

Once the beggars have received their fill and are filled with joy and delight, they in turn bestow gifts upon one another just as the Bodhisattva does; and as they pass on word of this to one another, it is just like the Bodhisattva’s practice.

The Bodhisattva’s fame for practicing generosity spreads everywhere, and all those who are poor and destitute come to seek refuge in him; just as travelers in the heat of summer all flock toward a tree in the wilderness, the Bodhisattva delights in this attainment of a superior state.
Why is this? Because they are able to cause those who seek alms to come, thereby enabling me to obtain the merit of giving; and by virtue of the merit of giving, they attain a superior state.
All sentient beings come to take refuge and gather around them; such Great Beings as these should all be paid homage.
When the Bodhisattva’s mind rejoices, he immediately perceives his body becoming light; by this sign, he knows that there will certainly be someone who comes to beg.
If someone comes and says to the Bodhisattva:
“There is a beggar who has come.”
The Bodhisattva rejoiced and immediately rewarded the messenger with wealth; he then gave the remaining goods to the beggars, looking upon their arrival with joy, love, and reverence.

When a seeker says "I beg," the Bodhisattva speaks these words with a heart of compassion. If there is a beggar who does not know the nature of a Bodhisattva’s delight in giving, the Bodhisattva takes their hand, speaks to them with joy as if to a close friend, and thereby destroys that ignorance, causing the sign of knowledge to arise within them.
When that beggar obtains wealth, he rejoices; seeing this, bystanders also rejoice, saying:
"May this savior of mine endure for a long time in the world."
"This is the true salvation for the beggar.

When a bodhisattva sees a beggar, his body and mind are filled with joy, and his face is like the full moon. He causes that beggar to be joyful and delighted as if nectar were being smeared upon his heart. With a gentle countenance and a compassionate gaze, the bodhisattva looks upon the person before him as if drinking nectar.
For example, if someone were to steal another's property and sell it in the market, they would feel great joy if it sold quickly;
yet when a bodhisattva receives a gift from a beggar, their heart feels even greater joy than that.

Just as a man of great wealth, possessing abundant riches and treasures and endowed with a thousand sons, might give them whatever they desire at their pleasure, out of affection and joy, this does not equal the great joy felt by a bodhisattva toward a beggar.
When a bodhisattva sees a beggar, his heart is filled with great joy, surpassing that of others who see their own kinsmen.
If he sees the other person obtaining abundant wealth and treasures, indulging as they please, and becoming self-conceited, the bodhisattva feels even greater joy upon seeing this.
When a Bodhisattva sees a beggar and hears their words, his thirst for giving becomes so intense that hearing those words is like drinking nectar.
If he hears the words of begging, a love and respect for them arises in his mind that nothing can destroy; yet if he hears the word "sufficient," that loving heart is destroyed.
A Bodhisattva always conceives thoughts of affection toward those who beg; however, if he hears the sound of "it is sufficient," the flavor of that affection is ruined.

The Bodhisattva observes the field of merit before him who receives his gift, wondering if there might be anyone equal to himself; he then sees that those sentient beings possessed by craving are indeed equal to him. Why is this so?
That greedy mind knows no satisfaction, whereas my mind of giving knows no weariness.
While that greedy mind covets great donors, the Bodhisattva, upon seeing many beggars, likewise gives rise to deep affection and reverence.
Those who are greedy always seek out donors with the desire to beg, while those who give always seek out beggars with the intent to bestow what they wish to give.
The Bodhisattva constantly acts as the giver to those in the world who act as beggars; they all approach the donor to beg, whereas the Bodhisattva approaches the beggar to give.

When a beggar hears that the donor's wealth has been exhausted, they experience great suffering and distress; however, when a Bodhisattva fails to obtain what is sought from a beggar, the mental anguish he feels exceeds that of the beggar by hundreds of thousands of millions of times.
Regarding those who beg, the bodhisattva reflects:
"The Buddha said that the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks is indeed just like this.
Thus, the bodhisattva conceives the thought of how difficult it is to encounter such seekers.

Why is this? If there were no beggars, the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) would not be fulfilled, and unsurpassed enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) could not be attained; therefore, one should give rise to deep compassion for those who beg.
If there is a beggar, unsurpassed bodhi will be held in one's hand without difficulty.
When a bodhisattva hears a beggar say, "Give me! Give me!", joy arises in their heart, thinking:
"This person is now bestowing unsurpassed bodhi upon me."
When foolish beings in the world hear of begging for wealth, they give rise to contempt and do not feel love or respect.
The Bodhisattva reflects:
"Those who are called 'beggars' are mostly foolish beings; because of their stingy minds, they attribute an evil reputation to me."
"Such a person as this may truly be called a giver.

Although one may possess wealth, if there is no mind of giving; or although one possesses the wealth and the mind of giving, if there is no recipient—if these three factors are fully present, such a person is one of great merit."

It is like a poor man who, upon finding a great treasure, feels fear that kings, thieves, water, or fire might come and seize it; yet when he encounters a friend who says to him, "I shall now employ various skillful means for you so that you suffer no loss," he is filled with great joy.
It is just the same when a Bodhisattva gains a beggar as a virtuous companion: his heart is likewise filled with great joy.
The Bodhisattva’s compassion pervades all places, and he feels particular pity for those who beg.
When the Bodhisattva sees a beggar with a serene and joyful countenance, he causes that beggar to conceive the thought that they will certainly receive [what they seek];
when the beggar sees the Bodhisattva’s face with such serenity and joy, they immediately give rise to the conviction that they will certainly obtain it.
When a bodhisattva sees a beggar, he says to them:
"Come; whatever you require, take as you please.
He comforts them with these words:
"Welcome, worthy one!
Do not give way to fear.
I shall serve as your place of refuge."

In this way, he comforted the beggars in various ways, constantly using kind words to bring a sense of cool tranquility to their minds, and gave them all manner of wealth and treasures according to their wishes.
The fire of craving in those who beg is fiercely blazing; the Bodhisattva constantly extinguishes this fire of craving through the gift of milk.
One who can practice such various forms of giving is called a living person; one who does not do so is called a dead person.
When the recipient of the gift obtains great wealth, and others see this and rejoice with praise, at that moment the Bodhisattva’s fruit of enlightenment is as if held in the palm of his hand.
When compassion is pure, giving is pure; if there is no compassion, giving is not pure.
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"One whose mind is well-tamed and disciplined honors compassion as supreme, for it is able to purify giving."

When a Bodhisattva sees those who are impoverished, his heart of compassion becomes exceedingly profound. When sentient beings who are extremely poor receive the Bodhisattva’s gifts, they immediately become immensely wealthy; it is as if someone were to obtain a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) and have all their desires fulfilled. When the impoverished encounter a Bodhisattva, all their poverty and suffering are entirely extinguished.

The bodhisattva first practices the giving of material wealth, next relinquishes those who are dear to him, then gives away his hands and feet, and further sacrifices his own body and life; in this manner, he gradually relinquishes things in successive order.
When a bodhisattva goes to where a beggar is and gives him wealth and treasures, he calls the beggar along with his relatives to give them as well.

If the beggar comes of his own accord manifesting the signs of seeking, the bodhisattva gives him his hands and feet; if the beggar speaks to request them, he immediately relinquishes his body and life;
and if the beggar does not come, the bodhisattva goes to him of his own accord to bestow them.
If one would even sacrifice body and life to those who come seeking, how much more so would one give away material wealth?
Having accomplished a heart of compassion, the bodhisattva never abandons it, as if it were his own very body.
When seeing a petitioner, the Bodhisattva conceives the notion of "another" toward his own body and experiences distress and fever within himself, thinking:
"How can one be so deluded as to conceive the notion of 'another' toward my own body?"
He said to the beggar, "All my wealth has already been given to you; it is entirely yours.
You should simply take it now—why do you speak of 'begging'?"
The seekers asked, "When will you give it to us?
The Bodhisattva replied:
"I previously made a great vow before the Honored One of the Three Realms, at which time I gave [this] to you.
Why do you now ask for it from me?

The Bodhisattva resolved that all sentient beings should regard his wealth and possessions as their own; just as birds and beasts come to the waters of the Indus River and drink as they please without anyone to obstruct or guard them.
Whether he gives or does not give, having first relinquished it, he no longer speaks of giving, nor does he give rise to a mind of joy.
Why is this? Because he has already given it away.
By means of all that they relinquish, they cause all sentient beings to attain happiness; for the Bodhisattva, all sentient beings are their messengers, and all sentient beings are their donors.

When the hearts of all those who are impoverished are fully satisfied, at that time the bodhisattva’s perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) is completely fulfilled; when the perfection of giving is fulfilled, one knows that merit is fulfilled.
When a miserly person sees a beggar, they turn their face away; when one who cultivates merit sees a beggar, they look upon them with joy and draw near, so that the beggar receives.
When a bodhisattva practices giving, seeing recipients giving to one another in turn, he gives rise to joy; all sentient beings likewise praise and rejoice.
Hearing their praise, the bodhisattva’s heart is filled with great delight, which surpasses even the bliss of attaining liberation.
When a Bodhisattva practices giving with a compassionate heart, he sees all sentient beings obtaining abundant wealth and treasures, becoming fully satisfied and happy.
Once these sentient beings have attained such happiness, they make this vow:
"We shall dwell for a long time within birth and death, cultivating various merits without seeking liberation."
When the Bodhisattva sees that sentient beings are able to remain long within birth and death, his heart is filled with great joy, thinking:
"I have now obtained a manifest reward; even if I were not to attain Bodhi, this would still be complete."
Chapter Five: Supreme Liberation. The Bodhisattva reflects:
"The one who is always beloved for supreme liberation has come to awaken me; he has not come for the sake of wealth or treasures, but has come desiring to bring my great task to fulfillment."
When a Bodhisattva serves as a king of men, those who have cultivated various merits may come and say to the king,
"A beggar has arrived.
The king then reflects:
"This beggar has come as a supreme liberation; I have now obtained him.
The King thought to himself:

"I do not now seek the throne out of greedy attachment, but rather because I desire to benefit all sentient beings. It is not right for me to occupy the throne in vain; I should cultivate the fruit of giving until it is fulfilled."
"Moreover, that messenger is one who awakens me.

Generally, it is very difficult for a beggar to maintain a composed countenance; harboring shame in their heart, their speech and expression change. The Bodhisattva, immediately perceiving their intention, spoke words of comfort:
"If you have anything required, seek it as you please."
Once the beggar has obtained the wealth and goods, his heart is filled with great joy; both the giver and the receiver rejoice together as if in the bliss of nirvana.
Within the blazing, great suffering of birth and death in the three realms of existence, the bodhisattva dwells as if in the bliss of nirvana.
Why is this? It is because he desires to rescue and deliver all sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva thinks to himself:
"To have compassion for sentient beings is my liberation.
To rescue and deliver sentient beings through great generosity, so that they obtain happiness, is my liberation."
"Even though one may perform great giving, if it is devoid of compassion, it cannot be called giving;
if there is compassion, then giving is itself liberation.
The Bodhisattva reflects:
"In the past, before the Honored One of the Three Realms, I heard and understood that liberation is supreme bliss; I have now realized it.
Why is this? To give according to one's intention is itself liberation."
If the bliss of the liberation of an Arhat were similar to the bliss arising from giving prompted by a compassionate mind, I would cherish it;
if it were not similar, I would not cherish it.
"Only the love that bestows happiness is considered liberation.

The joy obtained from giving with a compassionate heart is beyond compare; the bliss of liberation resulting from giving without compassion cannot serve as even a hundred-thousandth part of a metaphor for it.

If the joy and happiness obtained from giving with a compassionate heart could be illustrated by a metaphor, it would be so exceedingly great that no metaphor could suffice. Therefore, it cannot be compared.

Chapter Six: The Increase of the Donor. The donor who gives with a compassionate heart can bestow upon sentient beings a mass of happiness. For such a donor who grants happiness to sentient beings, this is superior even to liberation; it is called the most supreme.
A donor brings happiness to others; one who practices compassion and attains a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings is called a *dānapati*.
One who cannot give in such a manner is called a beggar.
If, when practicing giving, one causes those who hear of it to weep with sorrow, this is called "virtuous giving";
if it is not thus, one is not called a "virtuous donor.
If one practices giving such that the recipients and their descendants may enjoy it to their heart's content and praise it with joy, one is called a "mighty donor."
If one gives only when asked, they are not called a donor; if one goes of their own accord to give, they are called a virtuous donor.
If one gives away all one's wealth while still harboring a mind of attachment, they are not called a donor;
yet if one possesses a heart of compassion, even if they do not give material goods, they are called a great donor.
One who causes all those who come seeking desires to have their wishes fulfilled according to their original hopes is called a virtuous benefactor;
one who cannot fulfill their original hopes, even if they are exceedingly wealthy, is called a poor person.
If a wealthy person gives while lacking a heart of compassion, it is called "giving," but they are not called a "donor.
Giving with a heart of compassion is what is called being a donor.
If one does not consume [the gift], there is no karmic fruit; thus, although the gift was given, it is not called "generosity."
A gift given without a compassionate heart, though bestowed, cannot be called a true gift;
one who possesses a compassionate heart, even if they do not give, is said to practice giving.
If one who gives for the sake of seeking a reward were considered a giver, then even merchants could be called givers.
If one gives seeking a reward, the retribution is already immeasurable; how much more so for one who gives with a compassionate heart, seeking no reward—how can its retribution be calculated?
Giving while seeking a reward may only bring personal pleasure, yet it cannot provide relief and merely exhausts oneself;
one who gives with compassion is able to provide relief, and when the fruit is later attained, it will bring great benefit.
The poor are not equal to those who possess wealth; those who possess wealth are not equal to those who are able to eat; those who are able to eat are not equal to those who are able to give.
It is good for one to give with a compassionate heart. Among all sentient beings, the wealthy should practice giving, and the giver should act with compassion.
The wealthy who are able to practice giving attain firm and enduring wealth; those who give with compassion attain firm and enduring merit.

By cultivating generosity one attains wealth; by cultivating meditative concentration one attains liberation; and by cultivating a compassionate heart one attains unsurpassed enlightenment—the most supreme among all fruits.
Chapter Seven: Honoring the Beggar. The Bodhisattva reflects:
"It is because of those beggars that I am able to realize Bodhi; I shall dedicate this Bodhi to all sentient beings in order to repay their kindness."
"By means of giving to sentient beings now, I have attained incomparable bliss; because of this bliss, I shall attain Bodhi, and such Bodhi as this, I shall bestow upon the beggar."

Now, because of giving to those who beg, I have attained happiness and the bliss of supreme liberation; if even the happiness within the causal stage of giving is thus, how much more so the unsurpassed bodhi?
"I shall relinquish these and give them to all beggars.

Such beggars possess a most profound kindness that cannot be repaid; for it is such beggars who can provide me with the cause of great bliss. Since material wealth is insufficient to repay their kindness, I shall instead bestow upon them the unsurpassed Bodhi I have attained."
"By virtue of my merit, may these beggars also become great donors in future lives, just as I am now.
The Bodhisattva thought within himself:
"I obtain the joy of giving because of the beggars; therefore, I shall cause these beggars to attain unsurpassed bodhi by acting as a donor of the gift of Dharma."
When various seekers saw the Bodhisattva’s great giving, they asked him,
"For what purpose do you practice such great giving?
The Bodhisattva replied to each of them:
"I now do not seek the rewards of humans or devas, nor the nirvana of a śrāvaka; I vow to attain unsurpassed bodhi to deliver all sentient beings.
Those who are stingy and greedy will think to themselves:
"How can a bodhisattva practice such great giving without their mind becoming weary?"
The Bodhisattva replied:
"My teacher is the Honored One of the Three Realms, who compassionately regards all sentient beings.
Because I have no means to repay my teacher's kindness, I bestow [these gifts] without weariness."
Among all forms of happiness, there is none superior to the happiness of liberation; I love sentient beings more than I love liberation.
Because I cherish sentient beings and desire to bring them to liberation, I practice various kinds of giving.
"If birth and death were not ultimately suffering, I would never seek enlightenment through my giving; it is because birth and death are suffering that I give in order to seek enlightenment.
Who is it that brings about the uprooting of the suffering of birth and death?
Afflictions are produced by karma.
One should cause all sentient beings to take compassion as their essence and always delight in giving.

Chapter Eight: On Generosity and Stinginess. Those who do not acknowledge kindness possess no compassion; if one lacks compassion, one cannot practice giving. If one does not give, one cannot deliver sentient beings from birth and death.
Those who lack compassion have no friends; those who possess compassion can have friends.
One who calculates based on a self takes attachment as their essence, while one who provides relief takes compassion as their essence.
When there is deep love in the heart, no one can know it; likewise, when there is deep compassion in the heart, no one can know it either.

If one does not practice giving, that compassion remains concealed; it is like testing the authenticity of a stone by scratching it—it is only through seeing those in distress and suffering who are able to practice great generosity that one knows they possess a compassionate heart.
One who has much stinginess will turn even those close to them into enemies if they beg from them;
one who has much compassion will treat even an enemy like a dear friend.
One with a mind of great stinginess, though giving even mud and soil, regards it as more precious than gold and jade;
one with a mind of great compassion, though giving gold and jade, regards it as lighter than grass and wood.
One with a mind of great stinginess loses their wealth and treasures, and their heart is filled with great distress.
One who possesses great compassion, even when they have wealth and treasures but find no recipient for giving, feels a sorrow in their heart that exceeds even that [previous state].
There are generally two ways of relinquishing material goods:
the first is relinquishing them at the time of death; [the second is relinquishing them while alive].

Second, regarding the relinquishment at the time of giving versus the relinquishment at the time of death: that which is relinquished at death involves the total abandonment of everything, such that not even a hair’s breadth reaches the next world;
whereas that which is relinquished through giving involves abandoning a small amount of material things to obtain a great karmic reward.
How could any wise person, seeing these faults and perils, fail to practice giving?
When one practices giving, it causes the recipient to rejoice and oneself to rejoice as well; if a person cannot give rise to deep joy, they are merely deceiving themselves.
If there is a beggar who seeks something, and one gives even a small thing for the sake of their request, the mind is filled with joy.

Furthermore, there are those who go of their own accord to give, practicing great generosity without seeking karmic retribution; the happiness in their hearts at having some small remainder is beyond all comparison.
If one encounters fine food but eats it without practicing giving, one does not consider it delicious;
however, even if it is poor food, if one eats it only after having practiced giving, the heart is filled with joy and one considers it most excellent.
If, after completing an act of giving, there remains some for one's own consumption, a virtuous person feels joy and happiness as if they had attained nirvana.
Who would believe these words from one who lacks faith?

If there is delicious food and a hungry person stands before one, yet one cannot bestow it upon them—if such a person cannot even give away food, how much less could they bestow the supreme liberation upon others?
Even if one possesses abundant wealth, if one lacks the intention to give when a beggar comes seeking, how much less would one give a small amount?
Such a person does not perceive even a slight place of happiness within the cycle of birth and death, and thus cannot abide in Nirvana.

If a person, standing by a great body of water, cannot offer even a small amount of water as a gift, they will experience immeasurable suffering within the cycle of birth and death; do not remain therein, but rather quickly enter parinirvāṇa.
Just as it is not difficult for one who possesses abundant water to give it to others, so too it is not difficult for one who possesses a compassionate heart to attain nirvāṇa.

In the world, soil and dung are easier to find than water; yet a person of stinginess and greed feels such regret at the mere mention of being asked for soil and dung that they would feel even more so regarding material wealth.
Chapter Nine: The Giving of Material Wealth Suppose there are two people:
one is very wealthy, and the other is poor.
When a beggar comes, both of these individuals experience distress; the one who possesses wealth fears his solicitation.
"Those who have no wealth, how shall I obtain even a little wealth to give them?
Thus, although these two types of people share the same sorrow and suffering, their karmic results differ:

he who grieves with compassion will be reborn among gods or humans to experience immeasurable bliss, while the one who is stingy and greedy will be reborn among the hungry ghosts to experience immeasurable suffering.
If a bodhisattva possesses a heart of compassion, they are already fully endowed with it even before giving to sentient beings, let alone when bestowing even a small gift.

Just as a person of great wealth who possesses abundant treasures feels joy and happiness simply by directing their mind toward them according to their wishes, the sorrowful distress felt by a bodhisattva when contemplating the act of giving out of compassion exceeds that person’s joy by hundreds of thousands of millions of times.
One who possesses a compassionate heart may have no wealth; when seeing someone beg, they cannot bear to say "I have nothing" and fall into tears out of sorrow.
If one sees those in suffering and distress yet cannot shed a tear, how can they be called a practitioner of compassion?

If even when hearing of the suffering of others, the Victorious One cannot bear it, how could it be possible that he would see the affliction of others with his own eyes and yet fail to provide relief? Such a thing is impossible.
When one possessing a compassionate heart sees impoverished and suffering sentient beings with whom there is no wealth to give, their sorrowful sighs are beyond compare.

When a savior of sentient beings sees them undergoing suffering, they weep and shed tears; because of these falling tears, one knows that their heart is supple, and the pure essence of the Bodhisattva is fully revealed.
How is it known that this is manifested?
When seeing sentient beings suffering, tears fall from one's eyes; for this reason, it is known that the essence of the Bodhisattva is pure and supple.

The bodhisattva’s compassion is like a mass of snow; when the mass of snow encounters the sun, it completely melts away. When the bodhisattva’s compassion encounters suffering sentient beings, tears flow from his eyes because of that mass of compassionate snow.
A bodhisattva has three occasions [for weeping]:
first, upon seeing a person who has cultivated merit and virtue, they shed tears out of love and reverence;
second, upon seeing sentient beings who are suffering and lack merit, they shed tears out of compassion.
Third, when practicing great giving, the Bodhisattva leaps with compassion and joy, even shedding tears.

Were one to calculate the tears shed by the Bodhisattva since beginning this practice, they would exceed the waters of the four great oceans. The tears shed by worldly beings out of grief when parting from their kin do not equal the tears shed by the Bodhisattva when seeing impoverished and suffering beings for whom he has no wealth to give.
When a bodhisattva enters the samādhi for rescuing sentient beings and accords with a mind of supreme bliss, inexhaustible treasuries spontaneously emerge, and all who beg naturally arrive.
A virtuous man is one who can give great gifts of wealth to beggars; once the beggars have received that wealth, they too practice great giving.
A bodhisattva is able to bestow wealth upon sentient beings to make them prosperous, and with a mind of equal compassion, he sheds tears like rain upon hearing the voice of a beggar.
When the beggar sees the Bodhisattva shedding tears, even though no words of granting are spoken, he knows that he will certainly receive it.

When the Bodhisattva sees the beggar approaching, he gives rise to intense compassion and suffering; when the beggar obtains wealth and goods, his mind gives rise to joy, which extinguishes the Bodhisattva’s compassion and suffering.
When the Bodhisattva heard the words of the beggar, he wept with such grief that his tears could not be restrained; only when the beggar said "enough" did he finally stop.
Having practiced various forms of giving until sentient beings were fully satisfied, the Bodhisattva then entered the mountain forests to practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
How can the suffering and afflictions of the three poisons of all sentient beings be extinguished?
A bodhisattva possesses manifold wealth, yet there is no one to beg from whom it may be given; why should I now remain guarding it?
Now I shall renounce them and leave the household life.

Chapter Ten: Renouncing All. In this tenth chapter on renouncing all, the Bodhisattva possessed great wealth, yet there was no one who asked for anything; even when he called out to them, they did not come. The Bodhisattva reflected:
"I must surely sever all fetters and afflictions (saṃyojana), for there is no one who comes [to beg]."
With a heart of compassion, the Bodhisattva, seeing all sentient beings surrounded by manifold sufferings, makes a vow to deliver them.

Whatever may be sought from the Bodhisattva, he relinquishes it all; there is nothing he will not give, desiring to seek the Buddha-wisdom in order to provide the supreme salvation for all sentient beings.
The Honored One possesses supreme compassion and desires to provide rescue and relief;
what would he not relinquish? One who possesses compassion will abandon even nirvana for the sake of others, let alone his own body.
What difficulty is there in relinquishing body, life, and wealth!

To relinquish material wealth is not as significant as relinquishing the body; to relinquish the body is not as significant as relinquishing *nirvāṇa*. If one can relinquish even *nirvāṇa*, what is there that cannot be relinquished?
When compassion penetrates to the very marrow and mastery in compassion is attained, it is not at all difficult for a Great Bodhisattva acting as a savior to practice giving.
This is the most intimate [relation] for all sentient beings, serving as the cause for them to turn toward happiness.

The compassionate one relinquishes everything, free from all weariness; as a true savior for all sentient beings, regarding enemies and kin with equality, what thing—even their own body and life—would they not give away?
All sentient beings value wealth and profit most heavily, yet they cherish their lives more than material goods.
For all sentient beings, it is easy to relinquish wealth but difficult to relinquish life;
the joy a bodhisattva feels when giving away all material possessions does not equal the supreme joy attained when relinquishing body and life.
He thoroughly knows the various flavors of giving; taking giving as his sustenance, he exists by means thereof.
To bestow happiness upon others, desiring to know the flavor of giving one's own body, he gives his body.
When one sees another begging for a limb, the joy in one’s heart surpasses the joy of giving away wealth.
Just as a person who delights in giving attains the joy of generosity, it does not equal the superior joy attained by a Bodhisattva at the moment of relinquishing his body.
Among the people of Jambudvīpa, those who beg for wealth and goods do so because they lack my merit; thus, there come those who beg for my very body.
For one who gives away wealth, the property depends on others and may not accord with one's wishes;
but for one who gives away their own body, I attain mastery and can give it as I please, independent of others.
This body is not firm or stable; it is a thing that quickly decays. That which is dear and cherished should be grasped swiftly.
Those who eat meat said to the Bodhisattva:
"If you now give us your warm flesh and blood as a gift, how shall we repay your kindness?"
The Bodhisattva replied, "If you wish to repay his kindness, tell others further:
'One who possesses a compassionate heart can give his own flesh; you may go and take it.'"
"If one can act in this way, that is truly repaying their kindness.
He said to the beggar,
"You have now taken my non-durable body for me, so that I may obtain a durable body."
Your kindness is exceedingly great; how can it be repaid?
In a future life, the fruit of my renunciation of the body shall be bestowed upon you.

For the sake of rescuing and delivering all sentient beings, I have relinquished my life; by relinquishing the body, one attains the Dharma-body, and by attaining the Dharma-body, one attains all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), so that all sentient beings may likewise attain this fruit.
"One who relinquishes this body attains the Dharma-body, and the Dharma-body is able to bestow benefit and happiness upon all sentient beings.
If one can contemplate in this way, how could joy and delight not arise, leading one to swiftly relinquish this body?
When the Bodhisattva relinquishes his body, he reflects thus:

"I act as a kinsman and friend for all sentient beings; since I have crossed over birth and death myself, I ought to deliver all sentient beings and liberate them from birth and death. For this reason, I now relinquish my body."
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"This merit of my self-sacrifice does not belong to the category of compassion for sentient beings; rather, it is used to nourish my own merit-dharmakāya."
When the mind is thus resolved, there is no sign of difficulty in relinquishing the body.
Because the Bodhisattva relinquishes the body for the sake of attaining the Dharma-body, he rejoices.

One whose craving is heavy may experience immeasurable joy upon acquiring great wealth, yet this does not equal even a hundred-thousand-millionth part of the joy of a Bodhisattva when relinquishing the body.
The Bodhisattva takes wisdom and compassion as their essence, seeking the Dharma-body for the sake of sentient beings.
When a Bodhisattva relinquishes his body, his joy surpasses the sovereign happiness obtained by worldly people as a Cakravartin King.
For instance, if one of the Kṣatriya caste breaks an enemy’s array and can relinquish his life to be reborn in the heavens, he experiences immeasurable joy at the moment of relinquishing his life;
yet the joy of a Bodhisattva when relinquishing his life through wisdom and compassion is most supreme, exceeding even that.

Ordinary, foolish sentient beings, for the sake of wealth and profit, cast away their lives in the midst of enemy ranks; or for the sake of liberation, they lose their bodies countless times by leaping from cliffs or rushing into fire. How much more so should a Bodhisattva, out of wisdom and compassion, not sacrifice his life for the sake of all beings?

If deluded sentient beings sacrifice their lives for the sake of a kingdom out of a mind of attachment, how much less difficult is it for a Bodhisattva, through wisdom and compassion, to sacrifice his own life for the sake of others?
When a bodhisattva makes a vow, they renounce everything; although there is this statement, all sentient beings have not yet actually obtained benefit.
When they practice generosity, at that time all sentient beings obtain benefit and enjoy its fruits.

For a bodhisattva, it is not difficult to relinquish the body; rather, it is difficult to know that the body is impermanent, suffering, empty, and impure, yet not abandon it for the sake of sentient beings.

For a Bodhisattva, it is not difficult to sacrifice one's own body for the sake of sentient beings out of compassion; rather, it is difficult to find joy in such giving without ever feeling weary or satisfied.
Suppose one were to command an ordinary person to turn back the great earth; if they lacked the strength to accomplish this, they would experience profound distress.
Yet when a Bodhisattva sees suffering beings who have not yet been delivered, the sorrow and anguish in their heart exceed even that.

Because of their compassionate heart, Bodhisattvas regard their own bodies as lighter than grass or soil; thus, what difficulty could there be in sacrificing their bodies for the sake of sentient beings?
If a person, for the sake of their own body, observes the precept against killing for even a single thought-moment, that person will surely be reborn in the heavens upon the end of their life.

However, when a Bodhisattva sacrifices their body and life for the sake of sentient beings, all such merit has no place within the cycle of birth and death to be received; it can only be contained upon reaching Bodhi.
When a bodhisattva hears that someone has come to beg for his body, he immediately gives rise to this thought:
"I have long since relinquished this body and do not grasp at it myself; yet now they seek it from me, surely thinking that I possess a mind of stinginess and thus testing me."

11. Chapter Eleven: On Relinquishing the Aggregates and Receiving the Aggregates. An Arhat relinquishes his final body and attains the bliss of nirvana, yet this does not equal the bliss experienced by a Bodhisattva when relinquishing his body for the sake of sentient beings.
The liberation attained by an Arhat is not as joyful as the bliss experienced by a Bodhisattva when taking on a body for the sake of sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva reflects:
"Because I do not grasp at nirvana, I am able to receive this body for the sake of sentient beings; this is most excellent."
The Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"It would be most excellent if, having sacrificed my body and life as an offering, I were to undergo further rebirth rather than enter liberation.

I delight in hearing of the Tathāgata’s merit in saving sentient beings; having attained the compassionate heart that rescues beings, I take no pleasure in entering nirvana, for I deeply cherish this matter."

When a bodhisattva relinquishes his body as a gift for the sake of sentient beings, although he does not realize nirvāṇa himself, he excels those who have attained it, because he has not yet experienced the flavor of relinquishing his body for the sake of sentient beings.

For a Bodhisattva, receiving this aggregate-body (skandha-kāya) is an extreme suffering; yet when he relinquishes his body for the sake of sentient beings, that joy is no different from [the absence of] suffering.
Ordinary people of the world, being entangled and oppressed by the sufferings of poverty and illness, are unable to relinquish them, even though they desire to do so.
When sentient beings grow weary of and distressed by the aggregate-body and find no means of deliverance, they wish to enter *nirvāṇa* quickly.
The Bodhisattva reflects:
"Nirvana is supreme bliss, while the aggregates of birth and death are the greatest suffering.
I shall, on behalf of all sentient beings, undergo the suffering of these aggregates so that they may attain liberation."
"The body of an Arhat is exhausted, and the body of a Buddha is also exhausted; though their exhaustion of the body is the same, they cannot provide salvation.

It is for the sake of goodness that the Buddha’s body perishes. Chapter Twelve: Relinquishing Body and Life. For the sake of all-knowledge, and out of great compassion for sentient beings, the Bodhisattva relinquishes body and life; thus, the attainment of the fruit of retribution is not in vain.
If one were to relinquish the body without obtaining any karmic fruit, it would be called a "vain relinquishment of the body.
When a Bodhisattva relinquishes the body, it is because they wish to cause sentient beings who are attached to wealth to feel shame.
For a bodhisattva to sacrifice body and life for the sake of sentient beings is easier than for a miserly and greedy person to give up a single morsel of food.
That a bodhisattva sacrifices body and life causes shame to arise in those who are miserly and greedy.
The reason a bodhisattva gives up his own life is to protect the lives of others.
Why is this? Because the lives of others are identical to one's own life.

Although a bodhisattva may relinquish body and life yet fail to save others, this is because they perceive the faults of the aggregate-body (skandha-kāya); for the benefit of sentient beings, they undergo further rebirth.
Were it not for great compassion, what wise person would take pleasure in the aggregate-body?
If one lacks the flavor of giving born of great compassion, one cannot take delight in dwelling within birth and death.
A bodhisattva always delights in practicing giving; with mastery over great compassion, they undergo the body of birth and death at will, experiencing it as the bliss of nirvana.
Chapter Thirteen: Manifesting Compassion The Bodhisattva’s compassion is exceedingly great; it dwells within his person, yet none are aware of it.

When the Bodhisattva relinquishes his body and life, all devas and humans are thereby able to know it. The Bodhisattva’s compassion is profoundly deep and vast, pervading all sentient beings, such that no one can see it directly; yet through the giving of material wealth, the giving of the Dharma, and the giving of fearlessness, it is fully known and perceived.
The bodies of all sentient beings are nothing but illness, yet no one recognizes this; it is through three things that one knows they are ill.
What are these three?
Food and drink, clothing, and medicinal decoctions are themselves the manifestations of illness.
Through these three things, the Bodhisattva’s compassionate heart is made manifest. What are these three?
This refers to the threefold giving of wealth, Dharma, and fearlessness.
To bring happiness to all sentient beings and to extinguish all their suffering, the Bodhisattva sacrifices his own body to save them.
The Bodhisattva does not seek karmic retribution, regarding it as mere straw.
Through great compassion, the Bodhisattva employs various skillful means; thus, it is as easy for them to give their own blood to others as it is for worldly people to give water.

Just as in the past, when the Bodhisattva bled from five locations to give to the yakṣas and rākṣasas, he leaped for joy with an incomparable delight, desiring to rescue and deliver all sentient beings.
Another person asked the Bodhisattva,
"What is the flavor of great compassion that can make it easier to give up one's blood than to give up water?
The Bodhisattva Mahākaruṇācitta replied:
"Because they do not seek karmic rewards and act for the sake of others' happiness, they relinquish their bodies and lives.
Why is this happiness? It is because, with the signless as its foremost feature, they enter the joy of the compassionate mind."

When some people see the great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) of a bodhisattva, they suspect it might be the very essence of compassion; yet, because of his great giving, they know it is indeed the essence of compassion.
People of the world then give rise to doubt:
"Has compassion come and entered into the body of this bodhisattva?"
Why does the Bodhisattva enter into compassion?
When a Bodhisattva relinquishes his body, it is something that no one else can share; only those possessed of great compassion can do so.
When he attains the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), it is likewise something that no sentient beings can share.
Possessing a mind of great compassion for the benefit of sentient beings, one will obtain all that is desired without difficulty and will certainly attain emptiness.
For one whose heart desires to benefit sentient beings and whose great compassion is ever-present in the mind, unsurpassed bodhi is no different from being held in the palm of one's hand.

Those who have attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) can manifest *dhāraṇīs* and dwell in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*); their mastery should be known to be like that of a Buddha.

Chapter 14: On the Gift of Dharma (*Dharmadāna*). Regarding the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*), among human beings there are hundreds of thousands of millions of fruits of retribution resulting from such giving.

One can attain the gift of Dharma; only those possessed of great compassion can obtain the fruit of both the gift of Dharma and the gift of material wealth, attaining immeasurable happiness in future lives.
Through the gift of Dharma, the compassionate one realizes nirvana in the present life, while through the joy of giving, they are satisfied with the nectar of bliss.
The Bodhisattva’s compassion is of a single flavor; for this reason, he does not desire to enter liberation for even a single moment.
Having completed the various forms of the gift of Dharma, he requests those who have heard the teaching:
"When I attain the fruit of the gift of Dharma, you must surely accept my invitation."
The giving practiced when one is a bodhisattva is called "giving with desire" and is not the fundamental giving;
the giving when one has attained Buddhahood is called the "fundamental Dharma-giving.
Buddha-wisdom abides in the void, and great compassion forms the dense clouds.
The gift of Dharma is like a sweet rain, filling the pools of the sensory realms;
with the four means of integration as its skillful means, it is the cause for peace, happiness, and liberation.
By cultivating the Eightfold Noble Path, one can attain the fruit of Nirvana.
The gift of material wealth removes the physical suffering of sentient beings, while the gift of Dharma removes their mental suffering.

Through the practice of giving material wealth over immeasurable eons, one attains the fruit of the gift of Dharma; this gift of Dharma can bestow upon sentient beings the gift of fearlessness and brings about the ultimate weariness with birth and death.
The wise seek nirvāṇa; those who compassionately rescue sentient beings seek the gift of Dharma.
A bodhisattva accepts money and wealth for the sake of practicing giving, and when practicing giving, does so in order to attain the gift of Dharma.
He perceives that sentient beings are of two types:
those with excessive craving and those with excessive delusion.
To those with much craving, he gives wealth and treasures; to those with much delusion, he bestows the Dharma.
The giver of material wealth creates inexhaustible riches for others; the giver of the Dharma does so for the sake of attaining inexhaustible wisdom.
The giver of material wealth attains physical happiness; the giver of the Dharma attains mental happiness.
According to the beings to be transformed, he fulfills their desires for the Dharma as they wish, never wearying in his efforts to satisfy them.

Attaining great merit and the joy of the gift of Dharma, he increases in excellence; as upright as the full autumn moon, he is ever present before the eyes and minds of sentient beings without departing.
The gift of material wealth is beloved by sentient beings; the gift of the Dharma is always revered by the world.
The gift of material wealth is cherished by the foolish; the gift of the Dharma is cherished by the wise.
The gift of material wealth destroys the poverty of wealth; the gift of the Dharma destroys the poverty of merit.
Who would not revere these two kinds of giving?
The gift of material wealth can bestow happiness in the present life; the gift of the Dharma can bestow the bliss of the heavenly realms and nirvana.
Those who delight in compassion can love all sentient beings; to love all sentient beings is precisely to love oneself.
An Arhat abandons sentient beings to enter nirvana; such a one is not even loved by the wise, let alone those who suffer—whom would they ever cherish?
Constantly practicing generosity, staying far removed from the ten non-virtues, and honoring one’s parents—if one acts in this way, that is repaying my kindness.
If you wish to continue the lineage of the Buddhas, you should take compassion as your primary focus to benefit others, and always be mindful of accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings.
