Chapter Fifteen: On Generating the Bodhicitta. Regarding one who has fulfilled the practice of giving and acts as a kinsman to all sentient beings, there is not a single thought that is not in accord with compassion.

The Bodhisattva’s mind of compassion universally takes all things as its object, leaving nothing unobjectified; because this mind of compassion is all-pervasive, when he later attains Buddhahood, he realizes the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) without any obstruction.
Out of compassion, one abandons the liberation of the śrāvakas and gives rise to the bodhicitta.
This first moment of mind is such that only a Buddha knows its limits and measure; how much more so the joy of liberation through the practice of the bodhisattva path!
At the very first moment of generating the bodhicitta, it is like gold within the great earth; the soil of the great earth cannot serve as a comparison for it.
When the initial resolve is first made, it is able to purify all fetters and cause one to attract all merits.
Bodhi is the fruit of generating the aspiration for enlightenment; it seeks happiness for all sentient beings.
Once a bodhisattva has generated the mind of enlightenment, those who have not yet made vows ask:
"What is liberation?"
For what reason was this question asked?
Because one who has resolved their mind [for enlightenment] is as if coming from liberation, they therefore asked:
"What are the characteristics of liberation?"
"Is it known for the sake of going toward liberation,
or does liberation come here?
The one who had already made the vow replied:
"One knows this because at the moment of generating the bodhicitta, one experiences joy and happiness as if one were liberated.
Those who wish to make offerings to all Buddhas should generate the bodhicitta;
those who wish to repay the Buddha's kindness should generate the firm and steadfast bodhicitta."
Apart from the arousal of the bodhicitta, there is no other dharma capable of reaching bodhi.
If there is no bodhicitta, one cannot attain the fruit of Buddhahood; if one does not attain the fruit of Buddhahood, one cannot rescue and deliver sentient beings.
If one wishes to bestow immeasurable great bliss upon all sentient beings, one should resolve to attain bodhicitta. Why is this?
Because bodhicitta is the cause of happiness for all sentient beings.
All forms are not separate from the four great elements; all matters of joy are not separate from the bodhicitta.
How strange!
Why is it that you do not fear the suffering of birth and death, yet fear the fearless mind of bodhi?
If one wishes to bring an end to the suffering of all sentient beings, there is nothing superior to generating the bodhicitta.
Generating the bodhicitta is the primary cause for bringing an end to suffering; through this initial cessation, one attains supreme cessation.

The benefit of acquiring wealth and treasures does not equal the benefit of acquiring merit; the benefit of acquiring merit does not equal the benefit of acquiring wisdom; and the benefit of acquiring wisdom does not equal the benefit of acquiring the bodhicitta.
If one is negligent, forgetful, and fails to maintain the bodhicitta, one is no different from birds and beasts.
Why do you not now give rise to compassion?
You should know that compassion is itself great bodhi.
Those who wish to advance toward the wisdom of a Buddha should give rise to the bodhicitta.
Those obstructed by the fetters of afflictions (*kleśa*) cannot give rise to the mind of liberation; those obstructed by the retribution of karma cannot give rise to the bodhicitta.
What is the wrong course? What is the right course?
To be led by craving and to regard the four formless attainments as liberation is called the wrong course;
To resolve upon bodhicitta and cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path is called "rightly directed.

To obtain the retribution of wealth, one practices generosity; to obtain the retribution of happiness, one cultivates compassion; and to rescue and bring peace and joy to sentient beings, one should firmly resolve upon bodhicitta.
Those who do not cultivate merit encounter three things that are difficult to obtain:
first, they cannot draw near to virtuous friends;
second, they are unable to develop a compassionate mind of weary detachment.
Third, they are unable to revere and honor the Buddha’s wisdom.
Those who have not yet resolved to attain enlightenment (bodhicitta) should resolve to do so; those who have already resolved to attain enlightenment shall obtain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).

Chapter Sixteen: The Excellence of Merit In Chapter Sixteen, "The Excellence of Merit," it is said that when individuals offer material wealth as a gift to a single field of merit, they receive various kinds of retributions because their mental states differ—some obtain the happiness of the three realms of existence, some obtain the happiness of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*), and some obtain the happiness of benefiting others. Because the excellence of their intentions and vows differs, the retributions they receive are not the same.
Those who perform meritorious deeds with a mind of attachment will be ignorant and deluded when they receive their retribution;
those who cultivate merit with a mind of compassion will attain wisdom when they receive the fruit.
One should know that for those who do not let the bodhicitta degenerate and perform merit for the benefit of sentient beings, this merit is the most supreme among all merits.
Other forms of cultivating merit are called "similar merit" and are not the foremost merit.

One should know that cultivating the wisdom of the single flavor is the most supreme merit, for it benefits the world, ensures that the seeds of the Triple Gem are never severed, and brings knowledge of karma, knowledge of its fruits, and knowledge of taking refuge in the Buddha’s compassion.

When I calculate my practice of merit as being like the practice of evil, it is truly shameful; for a true noble person, seeing that the worlds of gods and humans are without refuge, would never cultivate merit for their own sake alone.
The suffering within birth and death is such that it cannot even be heard, let alone seen with one's own eyes.
Sentient beings receive bodies that are utterly loathsome and wearying; why then do you cultivate merit and perform deeds for my sake?

That which a compassionate person cannot do is to be separated from a mind of compassion for even a single moment while acting as a kinsman and friend to sentient beings; how then could one perform meritorious deeds for my sake?

For those who have tasted the flavor of merit, they attain the mastery to cultivate merit and gain the superior savor of repaying the kindness of others; such a person would not cultivate merit for their own sake even in a dream, much less while awake.

Through wisdom, one perceives the faults [of existence] and ultimately does not seek to cultivate merit for the sake of rebirth; through compassion, one never cultivates merit for the sake of liberation.
The wise abandon karma that seeks rebirth, while the compassionate abandon karma directed toward liberation.
Why is this? Because one who possesses compassion acts for the benefit of others with supreme wisdom and equanimity.
The fruit of merit from such causes is peerless; it is through this that one attains the knowledge of the Ten Powers.
To abandon the happiness of others for the sake of obtaining happiness for oneself is called being ungrateful.
Only I can know this; it is known through the Buddha, and therefore all sentient beings are my companions for cultivating merit.
If one were to attain the fruit and enjoy it alone, they would be called an ungrateful person.
Since such happiness is extremely difficult to obtain, how could it be enjoyed by oneself alone? Such a person is abandoned by all.

Even if one were to attain the bliss of a thousand nirvāṇas, it would not constitute true benefit; rather, rescuing the suffering of a single sentient being is superior to attaining the bliss of a thousand nirvāṇas.
One does not even enjoy the bliss of liberation alone.
Why is this? Because they see that the sentient beings of the world have no refuge and no savior.
They do not even seek to enjoy the bliss of liberation for themselves alone, much less the unsurpassed bodhi.

Chapter Seventeen: Supreme Liberation. Furthermore, there are other samādhis within the spheres of concentration and wisdom wherein sentient beings all become Buddhas; because they possess these samādhis, they do not desire to take up [the limited] liberation.
The dhūta ascetic removes all faults and evils, and his tranquility is as if within his mouth;
yet the true savior, for the sake of the suffering of sentient beings, does not realize [nirvana] for himself.
From concentration, wisdom, and compassion, he naturally gives rise [to these qualities], beholding the manifold sufferings of the world.
The true savior of the world never departs without having crossed over [all beings].

Just as the ocean tide never exceeds its limit, so too one who cultivates compassion may undergo ascetic practices for a hundred eons; yet if they can deliver even a single person, they will ultimately not themselves be born within birth and death.
By the power [of their resolve], they are able to attain liberation, yet for the sake of sentient beings, they remain within the cycle of birth and death.

Regarding the three kinds of giving, at all times they act as if it were a festival; they do not delight in their own happiness but bring happiness to others. Day and night, though amidst birth and death, they do not dwell [in attachment to them], but experience joy and bliss as if dwelling in nirvana.

The Bodhisattva constantly performs deeds that benefit sentient beings, possessing the wisdom of the flavor of joy and bliss; thus, even in dreams, the Bodhisattva attains a joy and bliss superior to that of liberation, and gains the flavor of the joyful and blissful spirit of bringing happiness to others.

While sentient beings generally do not obtain the flavor of liberation through realization, if a wise person attains liberation and experiences the joyous flavor of knowing how to benefit others, they will certainly return to bring benefit to sentient beings.

Those who fear birth and death and seek liberation for their own benefit as their ultimate happiness do not equal the Bodhisattva, who experiences joy and bliss at the moment of receiving the aggregates of the physical body for the sake of benefiting others.

If one could enter nirvana only after having personally experienced the suffering of oppression, then since all sentient beings experience the suffering of oppression, why would you abandon them to enter nirvana?

One who perceives their own suffering enters nirvāṇa; however, how could one who possesses compassion—perceiving the suffering of all sentient beings as abiding within their own heart—abandon those beings to enter nirvāṇa?
If one can bring joy and delight to others, that itself is nirvana; if one does not do so, that is samsara.
For those who possess impartial compassion for sentient beings, bringing joy and delight to others is nirvana—this is what the Buddha praised and taught.

If liberation were like the joy and pleasure felt when benefiting a single person, it would be cherished by the wise; however, if one bestows profound happiness upon others without calculating merit, that is true liberation.

The compassionate one brings happiness to others without expecting any reward; if one can act in this way, that is liberation. If one does not act thus, that is the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
To seek happiness for oneself is suffering; to relinquish one's own happiness to seek happiness for others is *nirvāṇa*.

Sentient beings in the world are called "liberated" because they have destroyed their own suffering; however, for one who cultivates compassion, to be able to destroy the suffering of others is the supreme liberation.
Since both parties attain happiness when another's suffering is destroyed, what wise person would abandon two forms of liberation to take up only one?
People of the world say:
"One who possesses wisdom attains liberation.
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"I do not believe these words.
How could a wise person abandon the joy of saving others to take up the liberation that consists only in obtaining happiness for oneself?
One should be able to bring happiness to others; the happiness within the three realms is surpassed by the happiness of liberation."
The Bodhisattva’s endurance of suffering for the sake of sentient beings surpasses the attainment of the bliss of liberation by others for their own sake.
Chapter 18: Benefiting Others. Worldly sentient beings, for the sake of their own pleasure, exhaust body and mind within saṃsāra; yet the Bodhisattva’s mind finds rest.

Within saṃsāra, apart from the practice of remedial methods (*pratipakṣa-dharma*), there is no other joy produced by a compassionate heart that benefits others; for the Bodhisattva, apart from benefiting others, there is no other joy.

A bodhisattva attains the joy and happiness of benefiting others, knowing that benefiting others is itself self-benefit. They relinquish attachment to their own benefit and delight in the happiness of benefiting others, knowing that the happiness of benefiting oneself is the happiness of benefiting others, and that the happiness of benefiting others is the happiness of benefiting oneself; for when one knows the happiness of benefiting others, it is simultaneously one's own happiness.
There are three types of people: superior, middling, and inferior.
The fool, when seeing others obtain happiness, gives rise to distress in his own mind;
the middling person, when he himself suffers, knows the suffering of others.
When a superior person sees others experience happiness, their own mind gives rise to joy; when they see others suffer, it is as if they themselves were suffering.
Among the Bodhisattva’s four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), this is "sharing benefits with others."
What is common benefit?
To feel suffering when others suffer and joy when others rejoice—this is called common benefit.

With a mind of compassion that is impartial and free from the notion of "other," the bodhisattva shares equally in the suffering and joy of sentient beings; yet, the bodhisattva’s own person alone gives rise to particular distress.
Why is this? Because they are unable to rescue sentient beings from suffering.

Without observing the past or the future, they act in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings to create remedies that extinguish suffering; the Bodhisattva’s own intention is likewise identical to the intentions of others.
Worldly beings provide benefit and happiness to others while still hoping for a return; the Bodhisattva provides benefit and happiness to others without expecting any recompense.

Although the Bodhisattva’s compassionate mind is impartial and loves all sentient beings equally, they bestow even greater benefit and happiness upon those who are hostile and hateful; when bestowing benefit and happiness upon such enemies, their heart is filled with joy.
To feel joy at the time of relinquishing one's body and life is called equanimity; if it is not thus, it is called non-equanimity.
To bestow even greater benefit and happiness upon those who harbor enmity and hatred is what is termed the work of a compassionate mind.
A Bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of compassion equally toward all sentient beings, yet they feel redoubled pity for those who engage in unwholesome conduct.
It is, for example, like a wealthy elder who has but one son, whose love and concern penetrate to the very marrow of his bones;
the Bodhisattva’s love and concern for all sentient beings is likewise.

Just as a wicked son who does not wish for his father to excel over him is called ungrateful, all hateful and hostile sentient beings treat the Bodhisattva with a uniform malice; yet the Bodhisattva regards those hateful and hostile beings with a uniform mind of compassion.

When worldly beings receive gratitude in return, they give rise to joy; however, if a bodhisattva bestows benefit and happiness upon those who harbor enmity or hatred toward them, the joy arising in their mind exceeds that by many times.
When the sentient beings of the world are reviled, they feel great joy if the other does not retaliate;
when a Bodhisattva is reviled by others, his heart feels great joy.
Those who possess affection pervade all three realms, and the compassionate heart of a Bodhisattva likewise pervades the three realms.
A bodhisattva’s compassion for beings in the hells is not as great as his compassion for those foolish beings attached to the three realms.

While sentient beings bind themselves with immeasurable great suffering for the sake of their own pleasure, the bodhisattva binds himself with immeasurable great suffering for the sake of the happiness of others.
All sentient beings are identical in their single concern: they all desire to leave suffering behind and attain happiness. To bring benefit and joy to others is the supreme conditioned state.

That which benefits oneself is both a cause for compassion and a cause for joy; likewise, seeing that which benefits others gives rise to compassion and joy. One feels compassion because one seeks one's own benefit, and one feels joy upon seeing that [others] have attained happiness.

Regarding the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), they are the internal objects of intent for cultivation; regarding the four means of attraction (*catuḥ-saṃgraha-vastu*), they are called supreme because they bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings.

One who cultivates the four immeasurables is able to bestow both mundane and supramundane dharmas; this is because mundane dharmas, supramundane dharmas, and the four immeasurable minds all share the same single realm.
Why is this? Because they share the same purpose of benefiting sentient beings and equally attain the single fruit of unsurpassed bodhi.

One who possesses compassion is able to benefit others; one who possesses wisdom is able to practice relinquishment; neither gives rise to a mind of longing, nor does either give rise to a mind of superiority or inferiority.

Chapter 19: The Chapter on Surpassing the Giving of Suffering to Others. When a bodhisattva sees the suffering of others, it is the bodhisattva’s own supreme suffering; when he sees the happiness of others, it is the bodhisattva’s own great happiness. For this reason, the bodhisattva constantly acts for the benefit of others.
When ordinary, foolish beings see the suffering of others, they regard it as their own pleasure; seeing the suffering of others, they do not consider it their own suffering.
The noble person, however, takes their own suffering as the means to bring joy to others, and does not [regard] their own suffering [as an end].
Ordinary, foolish beings bring great suffering to others for the sake of their own slight pleasure;
the wise, however, undergo great suffering themselves for the sake of giving even slight pleasure to others.

Although those who perform evil deeds may experience great joy when they obtain great pleasure as a result of cultivating causes for slight pleasure, this does not equal the immense joy of a Bodhisattva when benefiting others with even slight pleasure; the latter’s joy exceeds the former many times over.
When a bodhisattva sees others suffering, he takes it upon himself; though his body undergoes suffering, he does not regard it as suffering, for in his heart there arises joy and great rapture.
Through the attainment of compassion, the bodhisattva gains mastery over bliss and is no longer oppressed by the various sufferings of the three realms of existence.

Because the Bodhisattva drinks the nectar of compassion (*karuṇā-amṛta*), he is not afflicted by various sufferings; because he is not afflicted by suffering, he is able to undergo suffering for the sake of others.
When ordinary, foolish sentient beings see the suffering of others, joy arises in their hearts; when they see the happiness of others, suffering arises in their hearts.
When a Bodhisattva sees the suffering of others, he suffers; when he sees their happiness, he rejoices.

When one who lacks compassion sees the suffering of others, it is like the extreme cold of the moon; when one who possesses compassion sees others undergoing suffering, it is like the scorching sun of midsummer.
Regardless of whether they are foolish or wise, when they see the suffering of others, they all give rise to weary detachment and the causes of sorrow and distress.
However, one who possesses compassion gives rise to deep pity and forms a resolute mind, thinking: "The suffering of all sentient beings is my own suffering."
The Bodhisattva reflects:
"If one cannot arouse great diligence, by what means could one destroy this great suffering?
The Bodhisattva shares the same benefit, suffering, and joy as all sentient beings; thus, he must exert diligent effort to achieve Bodhi.
The Bodhisattva reflects:
"Once I have attained Bodhi, I shall relinquish it to all sentient beings, returning once more into the midst of birth and death.
From the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment until the attainment of Bodhi, he again relinquishes it to sentient beings; yet, [that which is relinquished] cannot be apprehended.

For the sake of benefiting others, a bodhisattva practices the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) without ever becoming weary, just as the great earth supports all things without ever becoming weary.
One who acts for their own sake may still grow weary even while experiencing their own pleasure; yet a bodhisattva never grows weary while bringing happiness to others.
When a bodhisattva brings happiness to others, they perceive the sufferings of Avīci as the bliss of nirvāṇa; how then could they ever grow weary or disheartened by other forms of suffering?

If for the sake of bringing happiness to even a single sentient being, they would undergo immeasurable sufferings in the hells themselves, they would always act with heroic vigor to bring joy to others without ever becoming weary.
For what reason does one not become weary or fatigued while bringing happiness to others?
The Bodhisattva contemplates all sentient beings and perceives no sense of "other," regarding them entirely as oneself.
Sentient beings, being bound by the fetters and afflictions, desire to harm others in all circumstances;
those sustained by compassion, however, desire to undergo all suffering.
When a bodhisattva undergoes the suffering of oppression for the sake of others, it is like a sufferer’s longing for the bliss of liberation.

When the bodhisattva delights in taking upon himself the suffering of oppression for others, his great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) becomes pure. As he contemplates others’ suffering with wisdom, compassion abides within him; where compassion abides, suffering cannot remain.
Although the compassionate one is entangled by the suffering of all sentient beings, they give rise to joy for the sake of others' benefit and happiness, which surpasses even the bliss of liberation.
When a bodhisattva sees others suffering as if it were his own suffering, and desires to give his own happiness to others, he realizes that this state is superior even to nirvāṇa.
One who possesses compassion constantly desires to take suffering upon himself and to give happiness to others; thus, compassion and suffering cannot coexist for even a single moment.
When those who practice evil see the suffering of others, they wish to avoid it from afar; when they see others obtaining happiness, their hearts are not joyful.
When Bodhisattvas see the suffering of others, they do not wish to distance themselves; for those without attachment, there are no karmic actions of suffering whatsoever.
Why is this? Because they experience great joy upon removing the suffering of others.
A bodhisattva does not necessarily feel joy when bestowing great happiness upon others; rather, they feel great joy upon seeing others bestow even a small amount of happiness.
Why is this? Because such is their essential nature.
When a bodhisattva sees others obtain happiness, they themselves also find joy; seeing someone else bestow even a small amount of happiness upon another, how could they not give rise to rejoicing?

Chapter 20: On Loving Compassion (Karunā). If a person does not know that their own body and mind are constantly bound by extreme suffering, they will be unable to know the suffering within the minds of others.

One who lacks compassion commits no evil; if, upon seeing the decline or misfortune of others, their mind is not softened with sympathy, such a person is called an evildoer of the utmost degree. How could they ever remember those to whom they owe great kindness?
To one who is at the point of death, even excellent medicine is perceived as extreme suffering, just as one who has committed extreme evil perceives it so;
likewise, those lacking merit perceive the sweet medicine of compassion as something of extreme suffering.
If a person possesses great wealth and abundant treasures but consumes them all alone without giving to others, they will be censured by others;
likewise, though one may possess wisdom and extensive learning, if they lack compassion, they too will be ridiculed and rebuked by others.
If one sees suffering beings and finds it difficult to give rise to compassion, such a person is not a vessel for merit, just as a broken vessel is unfit to hold water.

One who possesses compassion, upon seeing suffering beings—even if unable to rescue them—will at least be able to exclaim, "Alas, how miserable are these beings! Seeing that beings are afflicted by the diseases of greed, hatred, and delusion, and are constantly oppressed and tormented by the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
How strange! Sentient beings have fallen into this great suffering!
The sentient beings of the world experience physical and mental suffering, constantly destroyed by their fetters and karma.
Alas, how strange!
When sentient beings in the world suffer from such oppression, how could a bodhisattva not give rise to compassion?
Their bodies dwell within a swift current, submerged in the inexhaustible and terrifying great ocean of birth and death.

Sentient beings are constantly afflicted by the suffering of suffering, the suffering of conditioned existence, and the suffering of change; if seeing even a single form of suffering is sufficient to give rise to the cause of compassion, how much more so when all three sufferings are present?

Ignorant sentient beings are constantly afflicted by hundreds of thousands of sufferings; if one should give rise to a heart of compassion upon seeing even a single suffering, how much more so for hundreds of thousands?

One should understand all the sufferings of the world: those who have not yet given rise to a heart of compassion toward each and every suffering should do so; those who have already given rise to it should cause it to increase, how much more so when it concerns the immeasurable?
If one hears of the various and immeasurable sufferings of the world, even stone should soften; how much more so would those with hearts not feel compassion?
If one hears the sounds of lamentation in the world, even withered trees should bloom; how much more so would those with hearts not feel compassion?

The suffering of the world is of one single flavor; those whose minds are supple easily give rise to compassion. For one who possesses compassion, the fruit of enlightenment is already within the palm of their hand.
When compassion is most abundant, the joy of benefiting others arises;
yet a person impoverished of compassion cannot partake of this joy.
The infant-like fool is enslaved by craving; thus, the heart of compassion turns away.
Once the heart of compassion has turned away, all manner of suffering gathers together.
One who is enslaved by craving dwells within birth and death, desiring to divide their own suffering and cast it upon others as they revolve through the cycle of saṃsāra.
One who possesses compassion shares the joy of cessation with the sentient beings of the world and departs [from saṃsāra].
One who possesses attachment delights in the three realms of existence; one who knows the faults of attachment delights in nirvāṇa; and one who acts for the benefit of others delights in compassion.
Those who have mastery over love always delight in the world for the sake of taking on a body for their own pleasure;
those who have mastery over compassion always delight in taking on a body for the sake of bringing happiness to others.

Those who are dominated by attachment always delight in their own pleasure and thereby bind themselves; those with a compassionate heart constantly seek to bestow happiness upon others and thereby bind themselves. Those dominated by attachment never grow weary in their pursuit of their own pleasure, while those with a compassionate heart never grow weary in their effort to bestow happiness upon others.
Those who are foolish and love only the minor self neither love themselves nor love others; yet the Bodhisattva also loves himself.
For a deluded sentient being, that which is constantly regarded as "self" is in reality the "other."

Chapter Twenty-Two: The Great Beings. Bodhisattvas, driven by a heart of compassion, are constrained by only one thing: they are constantly oppressed by the suffering that arises for the sake of others, and have no other concern. This is called the fulfillment of the accumulation of compassion.

To cast off nirvāṇa as one would cast off suffering, and to accept the existence of a body as one would accept liberation—to bestow worldly benefit and happiness upon others is called compassion (*karuṇā*).
To know the merits of nirvāṇa and the faults of saṃsāra, yet not abandon the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), all such qualities are entirely the merit of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Being free from desire in all places, taking nirvāṇa as one's essence yet not grasping at nirvāṇa, such a person is called a "valiant hero.

Due to the causal conditions of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), they are able to enter the cycle of birth and death, moving back and forth through it; they observe the exhaustion and cessation of all existence, know that sentient beings are suffering, and for their sake act as saviors and refuges. Holding great compassion in their hearts, they loathe their own bodies and seek the body of the Ten Powers (*daśabala*). In the sphere of great compassion, they attain the merit of abiding in the sphere of compassion.
Just as a Wheel-Turning Sage King, though he may have a thousand sons, loves only those who possess the marks and signs of excellence;
so too is the Buddha, for among all sentient beings, he loves those who possess a compassionate heart.

One who is able only to perform meritorious deeds, yet lacks wisdom and compassion, is called a "man"; one who possesses both merit and wisdom is called a "good man"; and one who cultivates merit, cultivates compassion, and cultivates wisdom is called a "great man."
One should look upon those who possess compassion; one should converse with those who possess compassion; one should pay homage to those who possess compassion, for they are endowed with all virtues.
Chapter Twenty-Three: On Compassion. Among the beings of the world—humans, devas, asuras, and others—their embodied existence involves manifold sufferings.
Only those Bodhisattvas whose compassion penetrates to the very marrow know that all wholesome dharmas have compassion as their foremost principle.
Wise ones should understand that just as the Siddham script is the foundation for all written characters, so too do all wholesome dharmas enter into compassion.
Just as all various colors enter into a single house, if one perceives the purity of space, one perceives the purity of great compassion; as space is boundless, so too is great compassion boundless.
The Buddha said:
"If you wish to see me before your eyes, you should revere Great Compassion;
if you wish to see me, you should contemplate that all within the three realms are undergoing suffering."
Because suffering is boundless, great compassion is also boundless; because suffering abides, great compassion also abides.
Where does great compassion abide?
It abides within the mass of various sufferings of all sentient beings—namely, greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as birth, old age, sickness, and death—together with its retinue, dwelling therein.
To possess a heart of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) that is able to know the suffering of others is called dwelling together with the Buddha.
There are three kinds of giving that nourish the body with all merits, like a wet nurse; this is called great compassion.

Chapter 24: The Chapter on the Purity of Giving through Compassion. Just as the Snowy Mountains give rise to all medicinal herbs, the Snowy Mountain of Great Compassion gives rise to the three kinds of giving.
Apart from compassion, there is no other dharma capable of bringing happiness to the world;
by taking compassion as its essence, giving can bring about all manner of happiness for the world.
The unsurpassed fruit of retribution is accomplished through these three kinds of giving, and compassion is the cause of these three.
Since she who is the grandmother of all sentient beings can give birth to a Tathāgata—who would not pay homage to her, the supreme and most excellent refuge for all beings?
The ability to give rise to the three kinds of giving is called great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

Although the bodhisattva’s merit of great compassion dwells extensively within the mind, there is one thing from which he never departs and to which he remains entirely unattached: he constantly performs deeds for the benefit of others without weariness or fatigue.

The happiness of the world and the supramundane, as well as the happiness of benefiting others, all arise from compassion; therefore, I now revere compassion and those who possess the great compassion that benefits the world.
I also revere various merits; indeed, as it has been said, there are two supreme merits:
the ability to benefit others and the purification of one's own compassion.
Compassion can purify giving; therefore, I now cherish and revere it.
Generosity can adorn compassion, which I also love and revere;
I likewise love and revere those who possess compassion and share its resonant voice.

Compassion can purify the essence of the mind, and generosity can purify the path of karma; that which can purify the essence of the mind and purify the path of karma is able to purify the path to nirvana and purify the path to unsurpassed bodhi.
Compassion can purify equanimity; for one who lacks compassion, equanimity is defiled.
Generosity can purify compassion, and compassion can purify generosity; this is called worldly beauty.
Compassion can give rise to faith and reverence, just as the great earth is adorned by various flowers;
so too is great compassion.

When the sentient beings of the world are scorched and oppressed by the sun of afflictions, those who obtain a compassionate heart experience coolness and joy, just as during the heat of summer, one finds relief through a cool breeze.

Chapter Twenty-Five: The Excellence of Loving-Kindness and Compassion Taking is conditioned by craving; craving is the condition for taking. Where there is craving, there is taking; where there is no craving, there is no taking.
Where there is compassion, there is necessarily relinquishment; where there is no compassion, there is also no relinquishment.
Through attachment, grasping increases; through renunciation, compassion increases.
Attachment toward those who have been kind gives rise to further affection, which is a source of affliction; whereas toward an enemy, it increases the mind of compassion.
When attachment increases for the sake of one’s own pleasure, it harms others; when compassion increases, one is able to bestow happiness upon others while undergoing suffering oneself.
It is not rare for one whose attachment increases to cause harm to others; however, it is rare for one with a compassionate heart to give up their own body and life for the sake of another.
Those who are attached to worldly things are called foolish and base, constantly remaining in poverty and undergoing all manner of suffering;
those who possess the merit of compassion always abide in wealth and honor.
Those who possess craving can bring it to an end; when there is a time for contentment, one who attains wisdom is able to sever that craving through contentment.
However, those who have attained a heart of compassion never reach a point of contentment, because they constantly bestow gifts upon others.
One who possesses a heart of love (*maitrī-citta*) can summon all sufferings to form a great mass of suffering; one who possesses a heart of compassion (*karuṇā-citta*) can give rise to all merits.
If compassion does not abandon impure karma, that is not what I desire;
even if compassion cannot provide rescue and relief, that too is not what I desire.
If one who possesses compassion does not joyfully seek bodhi, that too is not what I desire.
A mind of attachment gives rise to all suffering, while a mind of compassion gives rise to all happiness.
The physical and vocal actions arising from compassion are called superior karma; one who possesses a compassionate mind can bring inexhaustible happiness to all sentient beings.
Chapter Twenty-Six: Wisdom, Compassion, and Liberation. Regarding the two matters of wisdom and compassion, which is superior?
The wise can only take refuge for themselves; the compassionate can cause others to take refuge in the unsurpassed path.
Compassion without wisdom is not cherished by the wise, nor is wisdom without compassion; both can obstruct the unsurpassed path.
If wisdom is not conjoined with compassion, it can obstruct the wisdom of the unsurpassed path; therefore, the Bodhisattva regards such [wisdom] as non-wisdom.
In a single thought-moment, he does not delight in birth and death, yet out of compassion, he does not seek liberation.

The flavor of liberation is like nectar, yet to those possessed of compassion it seems tasteless; just as fine food is considered tasteless without salt, so too, though liberation is sweet, a bodhisattva who lacks a heart of compassion regards it as tasteless.
If great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is distinct from liberation (*vimukti*) and individual liberation (*prātimokṣa*), both should be venerated, for great compassion is the mother of all Buddhas.
Liberation is defined as that which is forever without remainder, wherein all phenomena are extinguished;
the mind of compassion is like a potent mantra, capable of reviving the dead through its incantation.

If one accepts that there is a continuous, uninterrupted succession of bodies, this is the fault of eternalism; if one grasps at liberation as a mere cessation, this is the fault of nihilism. Because he is free from these two extremes, he is called the Buddha who saves all sentient beings.
If there were no Buddha, there would be no liberation; if there were no compassion, one could not attain Buddhahood either.
Compassion can give rise to liberation; for this reason, the Bodhisattva adopts compassion.
The single entity that is the essence of compassion can perform two functions:
first, it can save sentient beings;
second, it can give rise to the Buddha’s seed-wisdom.
Chapter Twenty-Seven: On Making Vows The Bodhisattva reflects:
"All sentient beings share immeasurable kinds of suffering."
"I shall give rise to a heart of compassion to achieve all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) and extinguish the immeasurable varieties of shared suffering of all sentient beings.
Seeing all sentient beings submerged in the boundless and limitless ocean of birth-and-death (saṃsāra) suffering, the Bodhisattva attains a heart of equanimous compassion.
The infant-like and ignorant one who delights in liberation gives rise to a mind of renunciation, thinking:
"The world is a great mass of suffering; this gives rise to my supreme heart of compassion.

The Bodhisattva reflects: "I possess a heart of compassion, yet seeing sentient beings who have not attained the path to enlightenment, how shall I cause these beings to attain the path of liberation?"
The Bodhisattva reflected:
"In all the world, I possess the least merit; I am currently unable to rescue and deliver sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva reflected:

"I have acted as a great friend to the sentient beings within the triple world, yet these beings are constantly oppressed by the suffering of body and mind; I am now called one who lives a life of empty evil."
The Bodhisattva reflected:
"I have been born unable to shatter the suffering of the world and unable to benefit sentient beings; for what purpose, then, do I maintain this body?"
The Bodhisattva reflects:
"I am a kinsman and friend to all sentient beings; I shall nurture even my enemies and bring them great benefit.
Thus the Bodhisattva reflects.
"All sentient beings can perform for me the karma that brings about physical excellence, and I shall not cause even a single sentient being to harbor thoughts of non-excellence.
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"As for what is called 'benefiting others,' when one seeks the characteristics of another, they are entirely unobtainable; they are in every respect identical to oneself."
Why is this? Because benefiting others is precisely benefiting oneself.
Thus the Bodhisattva reflects:

"If there be any object of aspiration, may all the physical and mental sufferings of all sentient beings gather together at once within my own body, which I shall constantly bear for them, so that sentient beings may obtain happiness and not experience suffering."
The Bodhisattva reflects:
"I shall be able to endure all the various sufferings that exist within my path to enlightenment. Why is this?"
“Sentient beings are submerged in the ocean of suffering of birth and death, yet I am unable to deliver them.
The Bodhisattva reflected:
“Although there are heavy fetters and afflictions, the path to Bodhi is difficult to attain.”
"In this way, with only compassion and wisdom as companions, the mind will never grow weary.
The Bodhisattva reflects:
"The path traversed by the Sugata, I shall now follow therein."
"I shall now, within this world, bestow [benefits] upon sentient beings with a heart of compassion.
I should reflect: 'I am no different from them.
Thus the Bodhisattva reflected.

"I am now the refuge and protector of the world; I shall now give rise to the great vow of aspiration, cultivate the wisdom of great adornment as my virtuous companion, for the sprout of the Buddha-wisdom is about to emerge within me."
The Bodhisattva reflects:

"I desire to extinguish the suffering of sentient beings and enable all sentient beings to attain happiness; I wish to perform the work of all sentient beings, for I am constantly instructed and exhorted by a heart of compassion."
The Bodhisattva reflects:

"Even hearing of the suffering of birth and death causes weariness; yet because one who possesses compassion is able to endure the sufferings of the world, for the sake of that compassionate mind, one still enters the gateway of birth and death."
The Bodhisattva reflected:
"The suffering of birth and death is extreme and utterly loathsome; I wish to enter nirvana.
Then, the Great Compassion spoke:
"How can I abandon and depart while sentient beings who are suffering have not yet been delivered?
The Bodhisattva reflected:
"The conditioned is replete with suffering; Nirvana is the supramundane bliss."
"I now know that birth and death are conditioned suffering and that nirvāṇa is unconditioned bliss; with a compassionate heart, I always delight in the three kinds of giving.
The Bodhisattva reflects:
"I am deeply afraid of all states of existence (bhava), yet for the sake of saving sentient beings with a compassionate heart, I delight in dwelling within those very states of existence."
The Bodhisattva Karuṇācitta said to him:
"I shall cause you to dwell within birth and death; I will never release you. Why is this?"
"It is for the sake of repaying my debt of gratitude. The Bodhisattva reflected:

"Even for the sake of liberating sentient beings, I would not wish to eat this bliss of liberation; since compassion obstructs me and prevents me from eating, how much less so this unsteady pleasure of saṃsāra?"
The Bodhisattva reflected:
"Of all forms of bliss, the Buddha has taught that Nirvana is the foremost.
Although this Nirvana is blissful, my wisdom does not desire to depart from it."
"The reason the wise do not wish to depart is because of their compassionate union.
The Bodhisattva reflected:
"I now revere and honor Nirvana."
Why is this so? Because within nirvana there is no birth, old age, sickness, or death.
Although nirvana is blissful, being drawn by a heart of compassion, he cannot depart for the sake of sentient beings.
Compassion is the mother of all Buddhas; therefore, one does not abandon [beings] in order to head toward nirvana.
If I do not even realize nirvana while it is still approaching me, how much less would I cast aside sentient beings to head toward nirvana?
The Bodhisattva reflected:
"I desire to proceed toward Nirvāṇa, yet this Compassion is the Mother of the Buddhas; she has come to me to give me her milk.
How could I abandon her and depart for Unsurpassed Bodhi?"
"If I were not to provide benefit and happiness to sentient beings, I would not seek even that [for myself], much less nirvana.
The Bodhisattva reflects:
"I should not head toward nirvana, for it would mean abandoning sentient beings who have no refuge."
"Out of compassion, may I not realize nirvāṇa.
Nirvāṇa is the end of birth; if there were no more birth, how could I rescue and deliver sentient beings?
Thus the Bodhisattva reflected.
“There are two kinds of happiness for one who takes birth:
first, the happiness of saving sentient beings; second, the happiness of liberation.
Why should I abandon these two kinds of happiness to take up only one kind?”
The Bodhisattva reflects:
"All ordinary beings possess the nature of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) in common; all-knowledge is easily attained by ordinary beings.
For this reason, I cherish ordinary beings rather than liberation."
The Bodhisattva reflects:
"Wherever there are sentient beings who suffer, the mind of compassion arises and compassion increases.
For this reason, I cherish existence."
The Bodhisattva said to Compassion:
"May you cause me to attain purity and growth, and may you cause all sentient beings to fully attain purity and fully attain growth."
The Bodhisattva spoke to the mind of compassion, saying:
"Sentient beings are in suffering, oppressed by hundreds of thousands of miseries.
Today, cause these sentient beings to surely attain peace and happiness; assist me in accomplishing this task."
The Bodhisattva spoke to the mind of compassion, saying:
"Sentient beings are bound by craving and seized by death.
Seeing that the world is without refuge or reliance, I shall undergo all manner of sufferings for the sake of rescuing these beings."
The Bodhisattva reflected: "I cherish great beings;
seeing sentient beings fallen into suffering, I shall set aside the bliss of nirvana and exert myself in this task for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to those beings."
The Bodhisattva reflected:

"Those who have just rescued sentient beings, attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti), and obtained the definitive wisdom that grants them the prediction of enlightenment—those who have received this prediction, I shall now honor and revere."
The Bodhisattva reflected:
"The Buddhas have attained the all-pervading pure eye; let me stand before them with palms joined and request the Buddhas, 'I pray that you grant me a prediction [of my future enlightenment].
28. Chapter on Making Vows in Common, the Twenty-eighth. All the Buddhas of the ten directions appear before him for the sake of saving sentient beings; I now make this vow for Bodhicitta:
"Whatever tasks all sentient beings must perform, I am capable of undertaking for them.
The great compassion of all Buddhas proclaims 'Excellent!
to us. By means of all my wisdom and merit, may I bring liberation to all those who have no refuge."
Blessed One, may you cause me never to delight in a mind of inferior wisdom; Blessed One, may you cause me to be as you are, fully endowed with the ten powers.

If the blazing fire of the fetters and afflictions of sentient beings burns their hearts, may I extinguish that blazing fire of the fetters and afflictions of sentient beings with the water of the Dharma, crush the enmity of Māra, attain noble wisdom, turn the wheel of the Dharma, and destroy all the decay and suffering of sentient beings.
For every single sentient being that exists, I shall simultaneously turn the wheel of Dharma for them; all the merit I have created shall be dedicated to this end.
By means of this merit, may I attain the most supreme Dharmakāya, which, like space, pervades all places, and may I attain the two types of bodies to teach and transform the world.
May my merit be united with that of all Buddhas to bring liberation to those sentient beings who have no savior.

The various afflictions, through their distinct characteristics, produce suffering and act as the causes of suffering; may the merit I possess, by the power of wisdom, extinguish the suffering of sentient beings, and by means of this merit, may I cause all sentient beings throughout the realm of empty space to experience a single flavor of bliss, and may I always fulfill my aspirations.
The host of thieves that are the hindrances (*āvaraṇa*) can plunder one's merit; the world fears death, so by means of this merit, may I rescue and protect all sentient beings.

For as long as the world endures, may my wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*) likewise endure. Through my wholesomeness, may all the worlds—both mundane and supramundane—be entirely freed from suffering and attain happiness, and may I always bring all sentient beings into harmony at one time.
The Bodhisattva reflected:
"From this day forward, I shall always receive instructions and commands from those who come to beg;
from now on, let them develop deep trust in my person and harbor no other thoughts. Whatever they may desire, I shall satisfy them by serving as their attendant."
The Bodhisattva reflected:
"May it be that from this moment until I attain enlightenment, there shall not be a single lifetime in which I do not behold a Buddha.
The Bodhisattva reflected:
"From this day forth, throughout the long duration of my births and deaths, even when I do not behold the Buddha, may I not for even a single kṣaṇa be separated from a heart of compassion.
The Bodhisattva reflects:

"May I continue until the attainment of Buddhahood; may the various sufferings experienced by external sentient beings so intensely afflict my own body that I take them all upon myself; may my very body attain a compassion that penetrates to the marrow; and may my body, body after body, attain the liberation of Buddha-wisdom."
The Bodhisattva reflects:
"May my heart of compassion be like space.
Just as all mountains, rivers, trees, birds, and beasts dwell depending upon space, may all sentient beings at all times enter into my compassion."
I establish my roots of goodness by relying upon all sentient beings; I dedicate these roots of goodness of mine so that all sentient beings may attain the fruit of liberation.
All roads, bridges, boats, and locations are the common property of all sentient beings; likewise, may all my roots of goodness be the common property of all sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva reflects:
"Earth, water, fire, and wind are shared by all sentient beings; may the various virtues I cultivate likewise be shared by all sentient beings."
"By means of the roots of goodness I have attained through all sentient beings, I dedicate them so that all sentient beings may attain unimpeded wisdom.
The Bodhisattva reflects:

"May all the virtues I perform cause all sentient beings to leave the realm of Māra and enter the realm of the Buddha; may I attain wisdom such that the ten pāramitās and the Buddha-wisdom are ever present before me; and may all sentient beings attain peaceful happiness and an unshakable mind."
"May all the decline and afflictions of all sentient beings cause them to rescue and aid one another.
The Bodhisattva said to Puḍi:
"All sentient beings are obstructed by ignorance; they do not know their own suffering or the suffering of others. You should bring them to understanding and liberation."

When a Bodhisattva practices the perfection of giving by distributing pure water, they cause all sentient beings to eliminate the thirst of the fetters of craving and attain the compassion of the unsurpassed path.
"When I give this water, may I cause all sentient beings to be freed from the servitude of affection and attachment, and may they always attain sovereignty and the wealth of the Dharma."

May my merit be like a river, with a compassionate mind as its stainless flower and the observance of precepts as its bed; may my generosity be like a swift-flowing stream, removing the suffering of thirst for all sentient beings.
"May my heart of compassion remain ever like a great river.
The Bodhisattva reflected:

"My heart of compassion is like the ocean; pure precepts are like the tides; patience is like the waves; wisdom is like the movement of sea creatures; and loving-kindness is like water of a single flavor."

"May all that I give cause the ocean of a compassionate mind to be perfected; may the merit of my giving obtain the nectar of compassion, and eliminate the birth, aging, sickness, and death of all living beings.

Chapter 29: The Chapter on the Supreme Aspiration "If, when I arouse a mind of compassion toward all sentient beings and bestow upon them benefit and happiness, may my great compassion become firm and steadfast, and through that compassion, may the suffering of sentient beings be extinguished."
May all the sufferings of all sentient beings come to oppress me alone.
By the merit of this gift of fearlessness, may all sentient beings attain great compassion.
By the merit of my present practice of patience, during the future age of the sword and conflict, may I extinguish the anger of all sentient beings through my heart of compassion.
By the merit of giving food, during the age of famine, may all sentient beings obtain sufficient food and drink.
By the merit of giving water to sentient beings, may I accomplish a heart of compassion that dwells within the hearts of all sentient beings.
By the merit of giving clothing to sentient beings, may all sentient beings attain a sense of shame and remorse;
by the merit of the causal conditions of giving lamps to the Buddhas, may I, in the future, attain the Buddha-sun that extinguishes all darkness;
by the merit of giving eyes, may I, in future lives, cause all sentient beings to swiftly attain the Buddha-eye.
By the merit of my giving away my head, may all sentient beings turn toward the bodhicitta;
by the merit of the causal conditions of my gift of medicine, may all sentient beings eliminate birth, old age, sickness, and death;
by the causal conditions of the merit of my serving and providing for sentient beings, may all sentient beings attain the unexcelled, outflow-free state and accomplish the path to Bodhi.
By the merit and causal conditions of my offering of lotus banners and canopies to the Buddha’s stūpas, may all sentient beings attain lofty and supreme blessings;
by the merit and causal conditions of my offering of pennants to the śarīra, may all sentient beings eliminate darkness and obtain illumination;
by the causal conditions of my offering of the sound of bells, may all sentient beings attain the Brahma-voice.
By the merit and causal conditions of offering incense, flowers, and necklaces, may all sentient beings be cleansed of the filth and stench of the fetters, outflows, and afflictions;
by the merit and causal conditions of making offerings to the Triple Gem, may all sentient beings always encounter the Triple Gem without ever being deprived of it;
and by the merit and causal conditions of removing the fears of perilous paths for merchants while I was on such paths, may all sentient beings emerge from the fear of birth and death.
By the causal conditions of the merit from my delivering sentient beings from the perils of the ocean of birth and death, may all sentient beings cross over the sea of saṃsāra;
by the causal conditions and merit of all my pure virtues, may all sentient beings shatter the four māras and attain perfect enlightenment.

"I shall attain supreme enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi). Although I speak these words regarding sentient beings, I say them for the sake of comforting them; by this merit, may all sentient beings attain unsurpassed enlightenment, for the enlightenment of all sentient beings is my own enlightenment.

All sentient beings are obstructed by ignorance; may I cause them to attain unsurpassed bodhi. By virtue of these causes, conditions, and merits, may all sentient beings attain Buddhahood before me, and may I attain it last of all.
By the merit of my causes and conditions for wandering through birth and death, may all sentient beings attain Buddhahood;
by the merit of my cultivation of a virtuous mind, may all sentient beings attain the wisdom of a Buddha.
Should there be anyone who sees, hears, receives, upholds, reads, or recites [this], all shall create the causes for unsurpassed bodhi.

Desiring to fulfill the wishes and aspirations of all sentient beings, yet my own vow remaining unfulfilled, if I hear the sounds of lamentation from suffering sentient beings, by means of this merit, may all sentient beings attain Buddhahood and behold me with joy.
“If I were to cultivate various virtuous practices yet fail to cause all sentient beings to become Buddhas, I would not even take pleasure in hearing of it, let alone practicing it myself.
The Bodhisattva said to Guṇa:
“If you are unable to protect sentient beings and serve as their refuge, I likewise have no desire for you or your karmic rewards.”
Why is this? It is because one cultivates merit for the sake of sentient beings and not for oneself.
If all sentient beings were to be exhausted, my goodness would be like space; throughout the three periods of time, I bestow happiness upon sentient beings by means of the bodhicitta.

The Supreme Being gives rise to compassion and makes this vow; this is called the exposition of the compassionate mind, it is also called the fivefold exposition, and it is also called the salvation of sentient beings; collectively, it is termed the practice of the Great Being.
